title: Conserving Colonial Order: A Review of Laws and Policies for Conserving Pacific Salmon in Canada
content:
ABSTRACT

Since its emergence, conservation biology has been framed as a discipline focused on preserving biodiversity. Less often acknowledged is that conservation is shaped by cultural assumptions about how, why, when, where and by and for whom it is designed and applied. Failing to recognize these assumptions risks reinforcing unjust systems of power rooted in historical forces that continue to shape present-day realities. This is especially evident for Pacific salmon in Canada, where colonial management systems have disenfranchised Indigenous fishers for over a century. In this narrative review, we describe critical moments in this history, focusing on case studies from British Columbia and drawing parallels to the United States and Sápmi to illustrate the pervasiveness of colonialism in salmon fisheries management. We examine periods from pre-colonial times to the present, focusing on Indigenous fisheries governance, treaty processes, the criminalization and vilification of Indigenous fishers, Indigenous resistance and significant legal and legislative developments. Our analysis shows that states have frequently leveraged conservation needs to justify policies benefiting settler societies while disenfranchising Indigenous communities, legacies that continue to shape power dynamics within contemporary fisheries conservation. We write primarily to settler decision makers, fisheries scientists and managers and the legal community, who play critical roles in reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples. We highlight the need for Indigenous authority over conservation, state institutions directly accountable to Indigenous Peoples, sustained funding for Indigenous-led salmon restoration and management and the upholding of Indigenous laws as essential steps towards a more just fisheries conservation and governance.
